findings.headline: Performance Development Plan completion collapsed from 40% to 18% in a single year
findings.detail: Staff PDP completion dropped from 40% in 2024/25 to 18% in Q4 2025/26. The council attributes this to form and process issues, with plans to implement new appraisal systems from April 2026. However, the scale of the drop suggests underlying HR capacity constraints that process changes alone may not resolve.
findings.matters: Poor capability planning signals HR management capacity issues and weak workforce development. Failure to recover completion rates after April 2026 process changes would confirm the council lacks internal HR capacity.
findings.figures: Q4 2025/26: 18% completion vs 40% in 2024/25. Target not stated.
findings.quote: Still very low take up, only 18% completion compared to 40% in 24/25. New appraisal, objectives and learning & development plan form and guidance to be used from April 2026 which will hopefully improve figures.

findings.headline: Council decision reports regularly late; 3 of 4 quarters exceed 5% non-compliance target
findings.detail: Q2 saw 23.8% of reports submitted late, Q3 17%, and Q4 15%, against a 5% target. In Q4 specifically, 6 of 41 decision reports arrived with less than 5 working days notice. Only Q1 achieved compliance at 4.6%. This sustained pattern across three quarters suggests systemic pressure on governance/administrative processes.
findings.matters: Chronic failure to meet reporting timelines is a governance stress indicator signalling insufficient administrative capacity or process breakdown, both of which matter to lenders assessing organizational stability.
findings.figures: Q1 4.6%, Q2 23.8%, Q3 17%, Q4 15% (6 out of 41 reports). Target: 5% across all quarters.
findings.quote: Overall there were 41 reports for decision and only 6 of these reports were received with less than 5 working days notice.

findings.headline: Staff vacancies at 22% with heavy agency reliance in Adult and Children's Social Care
findings.detail: The council holds 34.78 FTE vacancies (22% of establishment) against a 21% LGA benchmark target. Vacancies are particularly concentrated in Adult and Children's Social Care, where the council now relies heavily on agency workers. Lack of on-island housing is identified as the primary barrier to recruitment and retention of permanent staff.
findings.matters: Agency workers cost significantly more than permanent staff, creating hidden cost pressures in the budget. Heavy reliance on agency staff in statutory social care services also creates service delivery and compliance risk.
findings.figures: 34.78 FTE vacancies (22% of posts). Breakdown: 17.44 FTE held due to part-time requests; 22.18 FTE active vacancies. Previous year: 23.14 FTE (14.6%).
findings.quote: Whilst broadly in line with the LGA benchmarked target of 21% we are still aware of difficulties and reliance on agency workers particularly in Adult and Children's Social Care

findings.headline: Prior year audit objection resulted in £19,464 of additional audit costs in 2024-25
findings.detail: The final audit fee for 2024-25 reached £173,313 due to £19,464 in additional audit work resulting from a member of public objection, partially offset by reduced expert advice costs on land and buildings work. The document does not disclose the nature of the objection or the underlying audit concerns.
findings.matters: Public audit objections indicate scrutiny of council accounts or audit processes and trigger material additional costs. This signals prior audit friction.
findings.figures: £19,464 additional audit costs; total 2024-25 audit fee £173,313 versus £159,778 core fee
findings.quote: the total final fee for 2024-25 was actually £173,313 due to additional work costing £19,464 as a result of an objection by a member of the public

findings.headline: Audit fee of £156,541 represents 2% of revenue budget, more than 20 times higher as a proportion than comparable unitary authorities
findings.detail: The proposed audit fee is £156,541, a small reduction from the £159,778 core fee in 2024-25. However, this represents 2% of the council's total revenue budget, compared to less than 0.1% in most unitary authorities. Cornwall Council's audit fee is 0.09% of its budget. The council explicitly notes this mismatch is not addressed in any government funding allocation.
findings.matters: Small council audit costs are disproportionately high and create ongoing resource pressure that is not offset by differential government funding. This is an efficiency concern escalated to Full Council by the S151 Officer.
findings.figures: £156,541 audit fee; 2% of council revenue budget; Cornwall Council at 0.09%
findings.quote: Although the fee has reduced slightly it is still a significant cost to the Council and is disproportionate to the Councils size, it equates to 2% of the Councils total revenue budget whereas in most Unitary local authorities it is less than 0.1% (Cornwall Council's fee equates to 0.09% of its budget)

findings.headline: Risk that Cornwall Council support costs drift from marginal cost to full cost charging
findings.detail: The council relies heavily on collaboration agreements with Cornwall Council for IT, finance, HR and other services. The register identifies risk that 'over time and with increased pressures on their own resources...Cornwall Council become less willing and able to provide the support' and that 'charging methods that only charged the marginal cost of the support may start to drift to full cost charging as Cornwall's financial position gets tighter.'
findings.matters: Unbudgeted cost increases in outsourced services would directly impact the council's already-tight financial position and make planned savings harder to deliver.
findings.figures: Residual risk 9 (likelihood 3, impact 3); Target risk 4
findings.quote: Many of the agreements were based on charging methods that only charged the marginal cost of the support – this may start to drift to full cost charging as Cornwall's financial position gets tighter.

findings.headline: Inter-island boating provision becoming unaffordable and unsustainable
findings.detail: Transport between the islands is 'becoming an increasing challenge, particularly during the winter months' with costs 'increasingly less affordable, and provision of non-tourist boating becoming unsustainable.' The council has limited control as all transport is delivered by commercial operators. Government is considering a freight study but no solution is yet in place.
findings.matters: Unaffordable inter-island transport directly threatens the viability of island services and the island economy, which underpins the council's tax base and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Residual risk 12 (likelihood 3, impact 4); Target risk 4; High-impact vulnerability for island economy
findings.quote: Transport links between the Islands is becoming an increasing challenge, particularly during the winter months but also for certain services year-round. The cost is becoming increasingly less affordable, and provision of non-tourist boating is becoming unsustainable.

findings.headline: High reliance on agency social workers with difficulty recruiting permanent staff despite salary uplifts
findings.detail: The council faces 'ongoing reliance on agency staff in Children's and Adults Social Care, and insufficient applications for care roles despite ongoing advertising and MFS uplifts to salary levels.' This creates additional financial risk as agency costs exceed permanent staff costs. Workforce planning shows a coordinated action plan is needed but remains incomplete.
findings.matters: Unplanned agency spending increases revenue expenditure and diverts budget from planned savings in Adult Care Services, which the financial sustainability risk identifies as necessary to deliver.
findings.figures: Residual risk 9 (likelihood 3, impact 3); Target risk 8
findings.quote: Additional financial risk due to ongoing reliance on agency staff in Children's and Adults Social Care, and insufficient applications for care roles despite ongoing advertising and MFS uplifts to salary levels.

findings.headline: Children's Services rated Ofsted inadequate with deterioration noted in March 2026, full inspection due Autumn 2026
findings.detail: Ofsted rated Children's Services inadequate in July 2023. Subsequent progress was insufficient until a 2025 monitoring visit showed improvements. However, the March 2026 monitoring visit noted 'a deterioration in practice.' A full Ofsted inspection is scheduled for Autumn 2026. The register identifies risks to children's outcomes, trust in the service, reputational damage, and potential government scrutiny from the Department for Education regarding the council's sustainability.
findings.matters: A deteriorating inspection trajectory creates reputational risk, potential for commissioner appointment, and possible additional government scrutiny that could affect the council's financial position and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Ofsted rated inadequate July 2023; deterioration noted March 2026; full inspection Autumn 2026; Residual risk 12, Target risk 12
findings.quote: The subsequent monitoring visit in March 2026 noted a deterioration in practice. The full Ofsted inspection is due in Autumn 2026.

findings.headline: Council relying on government Exceptional Financial Support with future repayment obligation
findings.detail: The council is dependent on Exceptional Financial Support in the form of a capitalisation directive from government to protect reserves. The paper states this is 'a short term solution' that 'will come with an increase in cost in future years as any capitalised revenue expenditure will need to be repaid.' Financial sustainability depends on delivering significant savings, particularly in Adult Care Services, to align spending with funding.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's actual financial position beneath the capitalisation directive and whether the planned savings are realistic and deliverable.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 12 (likelihood 3, impact 4); Target risk score 4
findings.quote: Exceptional Financial Support has been required from central government. This is a short term solution and will come with an increase in cost in future years as any capitalised revenue expenditure will need to be repaid.

findings.paper_title: Council of the Isles of Scilly Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: Auditors previously recommended urgent, potentially transformational action to address Adult Social Care overspends
findings.detail: In 2024/25, auditors recommended the council take urgent and potentially transformational action to address Adult Services overspends. The 2025/26 plan indicates these issues persist and auditors will assess progress and review the medium-term financial plan including planned use of reserves.
findings.matters: If Adult Social Care overspends remain unaddressed after a year, this indicates either inability or unwillingness to implement necessary changes, compounding financial weakness.
findings.figures: Ongoing Adult Social Care overspend identified as requiring transformational action
findings.quote: In 2024/25 we recommended that the Council needs to take urgent and potentially transformational action to address the overspends within Adults Social Care.

findings.paper_title: Council of the Isles of Scilly Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: Council approved for Exceptional Financial Support from the Government to manage budget pressures
findings.detail: In March 2026, the council was approved for Exceptional Financial Support from the Government. The auditors will assess whether the council's budget proposals for 2026/27 address the underlying financial challenges, including planned drawdown of the general fund.
findings.matters: Reliance on exceptional government support signals financial distress and limited autonomy. Lenders need to know if support addresses structural issues or simply defers the problem.
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support approved March 2026; planned general fund drawdown in 2025/26
findings.quote: The Council has been approved for Exceptional Financial Support from the Government in March 2026.

findings.paper_title: Council of the Isles of Scilly Audit Plan 25-26
findings.headline: Council projected to overspend by £1.2m with £0.9m of overspend in Adult Services alone
findings.detail: The council's 2025/26 budget monitoring forecasts an outturn £1.2m over budget. Adult Services accounts for £0.9m of this overspend as at Quarter 3. This continues the significant weakness in financial sustainability that the auditors identified in 2024/25.
findings.matters: A council with structural deficits it cannot absorb faces capacity constraints on service delivery and presents credit risk to lenders.
findings.figures: £1.2m total projected overspend; £0.9m Adult Services overspend at Q3
findings.quote: The latest budget monitoring report currently forecasts outturn as £1.2 m over budget which includes an overspend as at Quarter 3 of £0.9m within Adult Services.

findings.paper_title: CIoS Internal Audit Governance Cttee Report - June 2026
findings.headline: External audit has required internal audit to implement tracking of outstanding audit recommendations and implementation progress, to start in 2026/27.
findings.detail: Following an improvement recommendation from external audit, internal audit will begin including summaries of outstanding recommendations, their due dates, implementation progress, and reasons for delays in its progress reports. This new requirement was not previously in place and will be implemented during 2026/27.
findings.matters: The fact that external audit had to recommend implementation of audit recommendation tracking suggests the council currently lacks systematic monitoring of whether prior audit findings are being remediated, indicating potential audit follow-up discipline gaps.
findings.figures: Implementation scheduled for 2026/27
findings.quote: Following the external audit improvement recommendation that internal audit progress reports should include a summary of outstanding recommendations, their due date, progress made implementing actions and reasons for any delay providing assurance to the Council on the effectiveness of internal controls and timeliness of implementation – this will be implemented during the course of 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: CIoS Internal Audit Governance Cttee Report - June 2026
findings.headline: Budget management rated Limited Assurance due to staffing absences causing weak oversight of Adult and Children's services spending.
findings.detail: Internal Audit found that the absence of permanent Strategic Director and Heads of Service in critical services resulted in weaknesses in oversight and accountability for budget management. This led to adverse expenditure variances during 2025/26. Although new staff have been appointed, they arrived too late in the year to implement corrective actions.
findings.matters: A Limited Assurance rating from internal audit on budget management indicates the council experienced actual control failures in monitoring spending during the year, a direct governance red flag for lenders.
findings.figures: Limited Assurance rating (vs Reasonable Assurance on other audits)
findings.quote: the absence of a permanent Strategic Director and Heads of Service being in post to direct and manage the critical Adult and Children's services has resulted in weaknesses in oversight and accountability for budget management across the two services

findings.paper_title: CIoS Chief Internal Auditor Annual Report 2025-26 - Appendix 1
findings.headline: Risk management audit identified gaps in service-level integration and staff training despite Reasonable assurance.
findings.detail: A Reasonable assurance opinion on risk management was qualified by agreed management actions to improve service-level risk integration and deliver training to both members and officers. This indicates that despite an overall Reasonable opinion, the council identified specific areas where its risk management framework needs strengthening.
findings.matters: Effective risk management is essential for councils to identify and mitigate threats to financial sustainability; gaps in training and integration suggest those defences may be incomplete.
findings.figures: Risk Management: Reasonable assurance, Medium residual risk
findings.quote: actions were agreed by management to improve some aspects of risk management, specifically relating to integrating service level risk management and also the delivery of risk management training for both Members and Officers

findings.headline: Fairer Funding review settlement below national unitary average and fails to account for tax base volatility or collection fund deficits
findings.detail: Settlement increase of 11.16% over 3 years falls short of national average (15.3%) and unitary council average (17.6%). Settlement calculation assumes unrealistic housing growth of 200 new homes and ignores collection fund deficit (2.5% of resources versus 0.05% for typical councils). Council estimates requires £480k-£1m annual additional funding just to reach unitary average. No additional funding provided for remoteness and accessibility factors despite Fairer Funding review intended to address these.
findings.matters: Indicates structural underfunding at national level—not operational management issue but funding model failure. Explains why EFS is required and why local cost reductions alone cannot close gap. Suggests continued dependency on exceptional support unless funding model changes.
findings.figures: Growth 11.16% vs 15.3% national average vs 17.6% unitary average; needs £480k-£1m additional funding; collection fund 2.5% vs 0.05% typical
findings.quote: the financial settlement following the fairer funding review process has not delivered the increase in funding that had been expected

findings.headline: Failure to set balanced budget creates risk of s.114 notice declaration by S.151 Officer signalling financial inability
findings.detail: Document lists as direct consequence of not setting balanced budget: 'Risk that during 2026/27 a s.114 Notice is issued by the S.151 Officer on (financial grounds)'. S.114 notice represents formal declaration that council cannot fund spending. Consequences described as 'extremely serious' with 'destabilising effect on delivery of services and the organisation itself'. Risk of inability to enter new supplier arrangements.
findings.matters: S.114 declaration severely damages creditworthiness and operational capacity. Triggers statutory intervention. Council is explicitly flagging this as outcome without EFS, indicating how precarious position is without government support.
findings.figures: Potential s.114 notice issuance in 2026-27 if budget not balanced
findings.quote: Risk that during 2026/27 a s.114 Notice is issued by the S.151 Officer on (financial grounds)

findings.headline: Council faces two-year 'challenging' cost reduction plan with Adult Social Care timeline uncertain despite historical escalating overspends
findings.detail: Council explicitly describes required savings as 'challenging' over next two years. Adult Social Care cost reduction plan exists but 'will take time to deliver' and demand 'likely to continue', leaving resolution timeline uncertain. History of £370k-to-£897k escalation over two years demonstrates difficulty in cost control. Success of these savings critical to preventing ongoing reserves depletion and future EFS dependency.
findings.matters: Operational execution risk. Council's future financial stability depends on delivering reductions that have historically proven difficult to achieve. History suggests structural pressures exceed local ability to control.
findings.figures: 2-year savings delivery timeline; £897k current ASC overspend to be resolved
findings.quote: will require the Council to d eliver a challenging savings and cost reduction plan over the next two years

findings.headline: Forecast 2025-26 overspend of £1.2m would reduce reserves to unsustainable level without Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: Adult Social Care (£897k) and Children Services (£236k) driving total £1.2m forecast overspend in current year. Without EFS support, funding this from general fund reserves would fall below minimum level required by S.151 Officer and external auditors. EFS approval is described as 'only option' that maintains minimum reserve level while cost reductions are delivered over MTFP period.
findings.matters: Reserves provide essential buffer for demand shocks, emergencies and service volatility. Being at absolute minimum reduces financial flexibility and crisis resilience. Limited reserves increase likelihood of further EFS requests.
findings.figures: £1.2m current year overspend; reserves would fall to below-minimum level without EFS support
findings.quote: With the level of forecast overspend in the current year it will reduce reserves to an unsustainable level

findings.headline: Budget support will be funded through Public Works Loan Board borrowing at rates explicitly higher than standard council rates, with 20-year repayment
findings.detail: Capitalisation direction must be funded via prudential borrowing from Public Works Loan Board. Terms explicitly state rates will be higher than rates Local Authorities 'normally' borrow at. Minimum Revenue Provision (MRP) repayment required over 20 years. Borrowing costs already factored into 2026-27 budget, creating long-term committed cash outflows.
findings.matters: Council accessing expensive debt at premium rates signals credit risk premium. Creates committed debt service costs over two decades. Higher borrowing costs reduce resources available for service delivery.
findings.figures: PWLB rates (higher than standard council rates); 20-year MRP repayment period
findings.quote: the borrowing is from the Public Works Loan Board at an agreed rate which is higher than the r ate a Local Authority can normally borrow at

findings.headline: Council tax base collapsed 18.4% in 2025-26 creating £198k collection fund deficit equal to 100% of annual resource growth
findings.detail: Council tax base reduced by 26.8 properties (18.4%) in 2025-26, with 75% of this reduction attributable to second homes no longer paying council tax. Combined collection fund deficits (council tax and business rates) total £198,102—unprecedented for this council and representing 2.5% of total resources versus 0.05% for typical councils. This collection fund deficit alone accounts for entire year-on-year resource increase of £188,747.
findings.matters: Indicates structural income shock rather than temporary fluctuation. Tax base volatility at 50x typical rate represents high financial vulnerability. Directly erodes borrowing capacity and available reserves to absorb demand shocks.
findings.figures: Tax base reduction: 26.8 properties (18.4%); collection fund deficit: £198,102 (2.5% of total resources); deficit represents 100% of £188,747 resource increase
findings.quote: there has been a significant reduction in the tax base for 2026-27, the biggest change is a reduction in the number of properties forecast to pay second homes which equates to approximately 20 (75%) of the reduction

findings.headline: Adult Social Care overspend escalating 140% over two years with uncertain timeline for resolution
findings.detail: Adult Social Care overspend has escalated year-on-year: £370k (2023-24), £696k (2024-25), £897k (2025-26). Driven by increased use of agency and interim staff, reduced income from self-funders, and rising demand with increasing complexity of cases. Cost reduction plan exists but will 'take time to deliver' and demand 'likely to continue', leaving resolution timeline uncertain.
findings.matters: Largest service overspend demonstrates inability to control spending on core statutory service. Pattern of escalation suggests structural rather than cyclical problem, implying budget pressures will persist regardless of one-off actions.
findings.figures: £370k (2023-24) → £696k (2024-25) → £897k (2025-26); also £236k overspend in Children Services
findings.quote: overspend increased year on year 2023-24 £370k 2024-25 £696k 2025-26 £897k

findings.headline: Council cannot balance 2026-27 budget without Exceptional Financial Support in form of capitalisation direction
findings.detail: Council faces £800k budget deficit for 2026-27. Applied for and received in-principle government approval for Exceptional Financial Support via capitalisation direction allowing capitalisation of revenue expenditure. Document explicitly states without this support, council risks s.114 notice and statutory intervention from central government.
findings.matters: Lenders need to assess whether council can sustain core operations. Requirement for exceptional government support signals severe fiscal stress and unprecedented position for this council.
findings.figures: £800k budget deficit for 2026-27; £1.2m forecast overspend in current (2025-26) year
findings.quote: this therefore leaves a budget deficit of £800k for 2026 -27

findings.headline: Airport fees increasing 18% on passenger and landing charges to achieve full cost recovery
findings.detail: Passenger fees, landing fees for commercial operators, and all other charges are being uplifted. Passenger and landing fees face the largest increases (18%) to bring the airport to full cost recovery including all corporate overheads and capital costs. The paper notes the increase per ticket will be less than £4.
findings.matters: Airports on small islands are critical infrastructure and material revenue sources. Large fee increases may suppress usage and revenue, creating a risk that cost recovery targets are not met despite the uplift.
findings.figures: Pax fees 18%; Landing fees for commercial operators 18%; Freight 5%; increase per ticket less than £4
findings.quote: Airport – has proposed to uplift their fees and charges for 2026/7 as follows: • Pax fees 18% • Landing fees for commercial operators 18% • Freight 5%

findings.headline: Adult Services fees are significantly below national average and will require a comprehensive review that may trigger substantial increases
findings.detail: Benchmarking shows Isles of Scilly's adult care fees are £1,195 for standard residential care (vs £1,404 nationally) and £1,445 for complex care (vs £1,604 nationally). The paper states the council will undertake 'a further exercise to understand the full cost recovery and charges that need to be implemented, this may result in significant changes that will require engagement/consultation.'
findings.matters: Substantial unrecovered costs in adult services (a large budget area) represent a hidden liability. The acknowledged gap below national benchmarks suggests material fee increases are coming, with consultation required.
findings.figures: Standard residential: £1,195 vs £1,404 national average; Complex care: £1,445 vs £1,604 national average
findings.quote: the average cost of standard weekly residential care for England is £1,404 (compared to £1,195 for Isles of Scilly) and for complex care the average weekly cost across England is £1,604 (compared to £1,445 for Isles of Scilly).

findings.headline: Council has been operating services below cost recovery for years, with accumulated underfunding from mismatches between forecast and actual inflation
findings.detail: The council increased fees by forecast CPI of 2.6% in 2025/26, but actual CPI was 3-4% and pay rises were 3.2%. The paper states 'it is clear the Council has not been operating at full cost recovery for a number of services.' This accumulated gap is being addressed through the 5% uplift, which exceeds forecast CPI.
findings.matters: Services operating below cost recovery indicate structural budget mismanagement and erosion of reserves. This pattern is often an early warning of financial stress.
findings.figures: Forecast CPI 2.6% vs actual CPI 3-4%; pay increase 3.2%
findings.quote: fees and charges were increased by the forecast CPI rate of 2.6% for 2025/26, however actual CPI during the year has been between 3 and 4%, added to this, the pay increase for 2025/26 was 3.2% and it is clear the Council has not been operating at full cost recovery for a number of services.

findings.headline: Council is applying for Exceptional Financial Support and using fee resets as a condition of that application
findings.detail: The paper explicitly states that 're-setting fees and charges on a full cost recovery basis has been one of the actions the Council needs to implement as part of the application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).' This reveals the council is in financial stress sufficient to require government bailout support. EFS is a mechanism for councils facing exceptional difficulty.
findings.matters: For a lender, an EFS application signals severe structural financial difficulty and government intervention. This council is not self-sufficient and is dependent on central government support.
findings.figures: Application for Exceptional Financial Support
findings.quote: Re-setting fees and charges on a full cost recovery basis has been one of the actions the Council needs to implement as part of the application for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS).

findings.paper_title: Appendix B - Environment Fees and Charges 2026-27
findings.headline: Waste disposal fees raised to recover budget overspend from current year
findings.detail: Nearly all waste disposal and commercial waste fees are increased for 2026-27, with the council explicitly noting in the comments column that the increases are to recover a budget overspend. Examples include residual waste (£600 to £650 per tonne), asbestos disposal (£1,221 to £1,337 per tonne), and all commercial waste collection and bin fees. The pattern repeats across dozens of line items throughout the service.
findings.matters: A waste service budget overspend large enough to require systematic fee recovery signals forecast control issues in a significant council operation. A lender assesses budget discipline and forecast accuracy as core financial health indicators.
findings.figures: Residual waste increased from £600 to £650/tonne; asbestos from £1,221 to £1,337/tonne; commercial 1100L waste bin from £79.50 to £86.00/month (exc. VAT) or £103.20 (inc. VAT)
findings.quote: Budget overspend claw back

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: Special Educational Needs Education Health & Social Care Plans completed at 75% against 100% statutory target in Q3.
findings.detail: 6 out of 8 SEN Education Health & Social Care Plans were completed within statutory timeframe, representing 75% performance. The target is 100%. This is a statutory function with below-target performance.
findings.matters: SEN Education Health & Social Care Plans are statutory obligations; failure to meet timescales can trigger DfE action and indicates systemic capacity issues in a key statutory service.
findings.figures: 6 out of 8 plans completed (75%) vs target 100%
findings.quote: Special Educational Needs – Education Health & Social Care Plans completed within statutory timeframe. Number (%) Actual 26/25 6 out of 8. Target 25/26 100% 100% 100% 100% 100%

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: Council reports published late to decision-making meetings at 17% in Oct-Nov-Dec quarter, above 5% target.
findings.detail: In the 7 formal meetings held in October-November-December, 41 reports required decisions and 7 of these (17%) were received with less than 5 working days' notice. Four of these late reports occurred in the December council meeting. This represents deterioration from Q1 (4.6%) and partial recovery from Q2 (23.8%).
findings.matters: Late publication of council reports suggests governance process issues, capacity constraints, or poor management of the decision cycle; it undermines proper scrutiny and decision-making quality.
findings.figures: Q3: 17% late (7 of 41 reports). Target: 5%. Q2: 23.8%. Q1: 4.6%
findings.quote: Late decision reports to Council and committee In the period Oct/Nov/Dec there were 7 formal meetings held, these featured 41 reports where a decision was required, and of these reports 7 were received 'late' (less than 5 working days notice received).

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: Sickness absence in Q3 increased to 8.2% of working time lost compared to 6.89% in same quarter previous year.
findings.detail: Q3 sickness absence rate rose to 8.2% in 2025-26 from 6.89% in 2024-25. The council reports ongoing management of long-term absence cases and expects figures to drop, but current trend shows deterioration from Q1 (4.33%) through Q3 (8.2%).
findings.matters: Rising sickness absence increases staff costs through cover arrangements (including agency) and reduces productivity; levels above historical average suggest genuine health issues or underlying staff morale/retention problems affecting service delivery.
findings.quote: Sickness absence - rate (% of working time lost) ... Actual 25/26 4.33 6.2 8.2 6.24%. Prev Years Actuals 6.15 7.39 6.89 7.20 7.04%

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: St Marys Airport passenger numbers finished 2,539 below forecast by end of December.
findings.detail: For the first three quarters of 2025-26, passenger figures totalled 64,111 against forecast levels. By end of December, the council was 2,539 passengers below forecast, indicating shortfall in revenue from airport operations.
findings.matters: If the airport generates council revenue, a passenger shortfall reduces income; repeated underperformance against forecast may require budget reallocation or service cuts elsewhere.
findings.figures: 2025-26 Q1-Q3: 64,111 passengers; End of December: 2,539 pax below forecast
findings.quote: Passenger Figures. 2025/26 (First 3 Quarters): 64,111 ... End of December: 2,539 pax below forecast.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: Heavy reliance on agency workers in adult and children's social care despite recruitment difficulties.
findings.detail: The council reports 92% of counties are experiencing problems hiring adult care workers, and the council is heavily dependent on agency staff in both adult and children's social care. Lack of on-island accommodation is cited as a contributing factor. Recruitment and retention difficulties have been raised corporately on the council's risk register.
findings.matters: Agency staff are more expensive than permanent staff and create less control over service quality and continuity; high reliance in critical statutory services creates budget volatility and service risk.
findings.figures: 92% of counties experiencing Adult Care Worker hiring problems; 94% of councils experiencing recruitment/retention issues (LGA Workforce Survey 2024); 21% vacant posts
findings.quote: Whilst broadly in line with the LGA benchmarked target of 21% we are still aware of difficulties and reliance on agency workers particularly in Adult and Children's Social Care (92% of counties are experiencing problems hiring Adult Care Workers, see below) and Children's Social Care. Longer term solutions are being discussed and interviews are booked for DASS/DCS, Head of Adults and Head of Children's.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: St Marys Airport requires immediate capital procurement for non-compliant fire rig to meet regulatory requirements.
findings.detail: The council has identified an immediate need to procure a new fire rig as the current infrastructure is non-compliant with regulations. This is framed as urgent and necessary for operational readiness. The council notes that Land's End airport does not have a suitable rig for their requirements.
findings.matters: A fire rig is essential for airport safety and regulatory compliance; urgent procurement indicates the existing asset is inadequate and creates both a liability and an unexpected capital requirement affecting council finances.
findings.figures: Unquantified capital requirement for new fire rig
findings.quote: Infrastructure Compliance : Immediate need to start procurement for a new fire rig, as current infrastructure is non-compliant. Land's End does not have a suitable rig for our requirements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: St Marys Airport audit findings deteriorated significantly with new Level 1 findings and systemic control weaknesses.
findings.detail: The AD/RFFS audit found 5 Level 1 findings, 16 Level 2 findings, and 4 observations—significantly worse than 2023's 3 Level 2 and 10 observations. As of 15 January 2026, 1 Level 1, 19 Level 2, and 5 observations remain open. Key issues: change management challenges and inadequate training provision in SMS, human factors, and AD operations.
findings.matters: Deteriorating audit findings indicate operational control issues; Level 1 findings are serious and the expanding gap between findings and closures suggests underlying systemic problems affecting airport safety and regulatory compliance.
findings.figures: Initial findings: 5 Level 1, 16 Level 2, 4 Observations vs previous year (2023): 3 Level 2, 10 Observations
findings.quote: AD/RFFS Audit (Mid-October) Initial Findings: 5 Level 1, 16 Level 2, 4 Observations Previous Year (2023): 3 Level 2, 10 Observations As of 15/01/2026: 1 Level 1, 19 Level 2, 5 Observations remain open Key Issues: Change management challenges. Inadequate training provision in SMS, human factors, and AD operations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A Council performance summary Q3 2025-26
findings.headline: Adult social care assessments and reviews fell to 66.67% and 75% compliance against 100% statutory target.
findings.detail: Q1 2025-26 saw 86 assessments of which 66.67% completed within statutory timeframe; Q2 saw 60 assessments at 75% compliance. This represents significant deterioration from previous years' 97.8%-100% performance. The council is failing to meet its statutory obligation to complete these assessments within timeframe.
findings.matters: Adult social care is a statutory function and failure to meet statutory timescales can trigger regulatory intervention and indicates capacity problems in a critical service area.
findings.quote: Adult social care assessments and reviews completed within statutory timeframe. Actual 25/26  86 (66.67%) 60(75%). Target 25/26 100% 100% 100% 100% 100%. Prev years actual 97.8% 97.1% 100% 100% 98%

findings.paper_title: Appendix B WORKING DOCUMENT PLEASE USE Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: Next phase of Adaptive Scilly climate/coastal erosion project paused due to insufficient project management and construction capacity
findings.detail: The council has identified insufficient in-house capacity and expertise in project management and physical construction. The next phase of the Adaptive Scilly project (coastal resilience, funded by Environment Agency) has been explicitly paused pending capacity improvements. All new capital projects must now pass Council scrutiny including resource capacity assessment.
findings.matters: Project delays signal delivery weakness and create reputational risk; pausing suggests constrained capacity for any future capital borrowing; climate/coastal resilience projects are externally funded but delays may jeopardize future funding.
findings.figures: Paused phase 2 of Coastal Adaptation works (allocated Environment Agency funding for 2026/27)
findings.quote: Paused next phase of Adaptive Scilly project until capacity is in place

findings.paper_title: Appendix B WORKING DOCUMENT PLEASE USE Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: Ofsted rated Children's Services inadequate (July 2023) with ongoing risk of reputational damage and service failure
findings.detail: The council's Children's Services received an inadequate Ofsted rating in July 2023. A monitoring visit in 2025 found significant improvements but stated more work is needed to move to a higher judgment. The register identifies risk of significant reputational damage and loss of public trust. Recruitment of senior leadership team and permanent social workers remains in progress.
findings.matters: An inadequate social care rating signals governance weakness and control deficiency; it creates reputational risk and may trigger intervention; service failures can drive unplanned costs and financial penalties.
findings.figures: Ofsted rating: inadequate (July 2023); monitoring visit (2025)
findings.quote: Ofsted rated IOS Children's Services, inadequate in July 23... Therefore, there is risk of significant reputational damage to the Council and in trust and confidence in the service.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B WORKING DOCUMENT PLEASE USE Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: Insufficient affordable housing is directly impairing the council's and local businesses' ability to recruit and retain staff
findings.detail: The islands lack adequate affordable housing for permanent residents, creating recruitment and retention barriers for both the council (CIOS) and local businesses. The council is attempting to address this through two capital projects: 27 homes via Live West (due Summer 2026) and 10 units at Telegraph (Autumn 2025), plus Park House redevelopment (works to tender).
findings.matters: Persistent recruitment shortages impair service delivery and raise costs (as seen in agency staff reliance); capital delivery is dependent on external partners and funding, creating execution risk.
findings.figures: 27 new homes (Live West, Summer 2026); 10 units at Telegraph (Autumn 2025); Park House redevelopment tendered
findings.quote: The islands stock of housing does not include a sufficient number of affordable homes to house local permanent residents and their families, resulting in recruitment and retention challenges for local businesses, including the CIOS.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B WORKING DOCUMENT PLEASE USE Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: Ongoing reliance on agency staff in Adult Social Care despite Market Forces salary uplifts, driven by rising demand for residential and domiciliary care
findings.detail: The council faces increased demand for Adult Social Care but cannot recruit permanent staff despite offering Market Forces Supplement (MFS) uplifts to salary levels. The register identifies this as creating 'additional financial risk' due to the higher cost of agency staffing. Permanent staff recruitment remains unsuccessful despite ongoing advertising.
findings.matters: Agency staff typically cost 50% to 100% more than permanent staff; rising demand combined with staffing shortfall creates an open-ended cost pressure in a demand-driven service.
findings.figures: No specific costs disclosed
findings.quote: Additional financial risk due to ongoing reliance on agency staff in Adult Social Care, and insufficient applications for care roles despite ongoing advertising and MFS uplifts to salary levels.

findings.paper_title: Appendix B WORKING DOCUMENT PLEASE USE Corporate Risk Register
findings.headline: Central Government funding does not reflect the unique costs of island operations, forcing continual re-prioritization of spending
findings.detail: The council's S151 Officer identifies structural underfunding as the core financial sustainability risk. Central government does not account for the unique cost drivers of island operations—particularly transport—and the council has limited ability to raise local revenue. This forces the council to continually re-profile and reprioritize spending across all areas, creating chronic cash flow instability.
findings.matters: Structural underfunding means the council cannot rely on stable cash flow to service debt or fund services as planned; a lender needs to know whether the council's income is sufficient to meet its obligations.
findings.figures: Residual risk score 3-4-12; target score 1-4-4
findings.quote: Central Government funding not reflecting the unique challenges of the Isles of Scilly and the inability to raise local revenue sufficiently, resulting in a continual requirement to re-profile and prioritise spending in all areas.

findings.paper_title: Proposed disposal of Old Museum , Church Street ,St Marys
findings.headline: Building has been vacant and derelict for seven years with structural condition concerns
findings.detail: The Old Museum was vacated in 2019 due to structural concerns and has remained vacant and derelict for seven years. A replacement museum facility is currently under construction within the Town Hall redevelopment and is scheduled for completion later in 2026, at which point the council can proceed with marketing the Old Museum site.
findings.matters: Long-term vacancy of a significant asset signals potential maintenance liabilities, underutilization of the asset base, and potential delays in project delivery (the Town Hall redevelopment has taken substantial time to progress to this point).
findings.figures: Building vacated 2019; replacement facility scheduled completion later 2026 (seven-year gap)
findings.quote: The Old Museum was vacated in 2019 following concerns over the buildings structural condition. A replacement facility is currently under construction within the Town Hall redevelopment. That facility is scheduled for completion later this year.

findings.paper_title: Proposed disposal of Old Museum , Church Street ,St Marys
findings.headline: Capital receipt from asset disposal is required to fund Town Hall redevelopment capital contribution
findings.detail: The council is disposing of the Old Museum to generate a capital receipt that will be reinvested to fund its capital programme, specifically to provide the capital contribution required for the Town Hall redevelopment. This demonstrates the council is dependent on asset sales rather than other sources to finance capital projects.
findings.matters: Reliance on asset sales to fund capital programmes—rather than revenue or borrowing—suggests constrained financial resources and that future capital delivery may depend on successful asset disposals.
findings.figures: Asset valuation in 2022 exceeded £20,000 threshold; specific valuation amount not disclosed
findings.quote: Any capital receipt will be reinvested by the Council to help fund the Councils capital programme including the capital contribution to the Town Hall redevelopment

findings.paper_title: Proposed disposal of Old Museum , Church Street ,St Marys
findings.headline: Council explicitly states it has limited borrowing capacity despite significant capital programme
findings.detail: The council states it has limited borrowing capacity at this time while managing a significant capital programme. This directly constrains the council's ability to fund capital projects itself, which is why it cannot undertake the site redevelopment and must instead sell the asset to a private developer or registered provider.
findings.matters: Limited borrowing capacity directly affects a lender's assessment of the council's debt headroom, financial flexibility, and ability to absorb shocks or fund future capital needs.
findings.figures: Asset valuation exceeded £20,000 threshold; £182,000 from Homes England Small Sites Fund ringfenced for housing development
findings.quote: the Council already has a significant Capital Programme with limited borrowing capacity at this time

findings.paper_title: Commercial Waste Subscription Service Fees and Charges (2026-2027)
findings.headline: Full cost recovery strategy dependent on fee increases that may drive illegal waste disposal and fall short of target
findings.detail: The council is pursuing full cost recovery for commercial waste through a 5% fee increase. However, previous year charges have not delivered full cost recovery, requiring future combinations of further charges and cost reductions. Officers acknowledge increased fees risk incentivising illegal and non-compliant waste disposal.
findings.matters: The council's budget strategy depends on fee revenue that may not materialise if businesses respond to price increases by non-compliant disposal, undermining the intended financial solution.
findings.figures: 5% inflation increase: 90l residual waste sack from £6.50 to £7.50; recycling container from £2.00 to £2.50
findings.quote: The charges set for 2025-2026 will not deliver this entirely for one year and that a mix of further increased charges and reduced costs will be needed in future years to achieve the full outcome of full cost recovery. increased fees and charges for waste disposal could lead to illegal and non-compliant waste disposal by businesses operating across the islands.

findings.paper_title: Commercial Waste Subscription Service Fees and Charges (2026-2027)
findings.headline: Waste management costs rising and marine haulage contract expiring November 2026 with uncertain cost reduction prospects
findings.detail: Multiple waste contracts have driven cost increases. The marine haulage contract for transporting waste to the mainland expires in November 2026 and officers will attempt to negotiate significant savings with the incumbent contractor, but may require a competitive tender if savings cannot be made.
findings.matters: A key operational contract approaching expiry with uncertain cost trajectory creates ongoing budget pressure and planning uncertainty for an island council with limited disposal alternatives.
findings.figures: Marine haulage contract expires November 2026
findings.quote: Waste management costs have risen in other areas, primarily due to new off island waste management and Inter-Island haulage contracts being issued. The Council's marine haulage contract for the transportation of waste and recycling from the Porthmellon Waste and Recycling Site to the mainland is due to expire November 2026.

findings.paper_title: Commercial Waste Subscription Service Fees and Charges (2026-2027)
findings.headline: Waste service budget currently overspent with £60,000 of savings from Cornwall collaboration unachieved and now delayed to June 2026
findings.detail: The council anticipated £60,000 in savings during 2025-2026 from joining a collaboration with Cornwall Council for waste disposal. These savings have not been realised due to technical issues at the Cornwall Energy Recovery Centre, leaving the waste budget currently overspent. Recovery is now expected no earlier than June 2026.
findings.matters: A material service overspend with cost-saving plans delayed due to third-party infrastructure issues represents budget control and delivery risk that a lender would assess carefully.
findings.figures: £60,000 savings target for 2025-2026; expected recovery June 2026
findings.quote: The Council's waste budget is currently overspent because the anticipated £60,000 (2025–2026) savings in waste disposal have not yet been achieved. The delay is primarily due to technical issues at the Cornwall Energy Recovery Centre (CERC).

findings.headline: Children's Services must sustain improvement momentum ahead of full Ofsted inspection
findings.detail: Following an Ofsted inadequate rating in July 2023, the service has shown demonstrable improvement. October 2025 monitoring visit confirmed continued progress but noted the need to embed improvements, secure permanent leadership, and strengthen support for off-island children before the anticipated full inspection.
findings.matters: Continued regulatory scrutiny and the need for sustained investment in improvement creates ongoing financial commitment and reputational risk. Service delivered £0.780m overspend in 2024/25 with agency costs significant.
findings.figures: £0.780m overspend in Children's Services 2024/25
findings.quote: A fourth monitoring visit in October 2025 confirmed continued improvement, noting that children receive timely help and appropriate responses to risk. However, the report also noted that further work is needed to embed practice improvements, secure permanent leadership roles, and strengthen oversight and support for post-16 education for children living off the mainland.

findings.headline: Q1 2025/26 forecast shows £0.459m overspend (23% of opening reserves) and expected to worsen
findings.detail: Despite a balanced budget set for 2025/26 without planned reserve use, Q1 reporting already forecasts £0.459m year-end overspend, with £0.375m attributable to Adult Social Care. This represents 23% of opening reserve balance and is expected to increase further through the year.
findings.matters: Early-year variance of this magnitude signals budget assumptions are not holding and council will need to draw reserves within the year, continuing the pattern of unsustainable reliance on one-off funding.
findings.figures: Q1 2025/26 forecast overspend: £0.460m; Adult Social Care portion: £0.375m; represents 23% of opening General Fund Reserve
findings.quote: A balanced budget was set for 2025/26, without planned use of general reserves however, cost pressures persist in Children's and Adult Services and at Quarter 1, the Council forecast £0.460m overspend at year end of which £0.375m is attributable to overspends in Adult Social Care. This is expected to increase in year.

findings.headline: Savings targets severely under-identified for 2026/27 with only £65k secured
findings.detail: The council has identified only £65k of savings for 2026/27, equivalent to less than 1% of net revenue budget. This follows 98.5% delivery in 2024/25 (£0.421m of £0.427m) and forecast 95% delivery in 2025/26 (£0.499m). The shortfall relies on £0.273m of general fund reserves with no substantive savings plan to bridge the gap.
findings.matters: The significant gap between identified savings and requirement to balance budgets forces reliance on reserves, accelerating depletion and creating unsustainable dependency on one-off funding.
findings.figures: 2026/27 identified savings: £65k (less than 1% of net revenue budget); 2025/26 target: £0.499m; 2024/25 delivered: £0.421m of £0.427m planned
findings.quote: Looking ahead to 2026/27, the Council has identified only £65k in savings, leaving a significant gap which relies on £273k from the General Fund Reserve alongside the identified savings and requiring the identification of further savings to achieve a balanced budget.

findings.headline: General Fund Reserve will fall to near-minimum levels by April 2027 with no plan to rebuild
findings.detail: Opening balance April 2025 was £2.034m. Planned use of £0.273m in 2026/27 would reduce reserves to £1.760m. Minimum reserve requirement is £1.695m based on risk assessment. No strategy exists to rebuild balances. This leaves virtually no headroom for unforeseen shocks.
findings.matters: Councils at or near minimum reserve levels cannot absorb service cost escalations or one-off pressures without triggering financial emergency. This directly affects council creditworthiness and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Opening General Fund Reserve: £2.034m (April 2025); Forecast: £1.760m (April 2027); Minimum required: £1.695m; Planned MTFP use: £0.273m
findings.quote: The MTFP shows a £0.273m budget gap in 2026/27, currently planned to be funded from the general fund reserve, further reducing resilience. There are currently no plans to rebuild balances, and if overspends in ASC continue to escalate there is a risk that reserves balances will soon become depleted.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care costs creating unsustainable overspends with significant weakness identified by auditors
findings.detail: The Council reported £0.696m Adult Social Care overspend in 2024/25 and faces escalating costs in 2025/26. Q1 2025/26 shows a further £0.375m overspend driven by increased reliance on agency staff and increased travel and accommodation costs. The auditors identified a significant weakness in financial sustainability and issued a key recommendation for urgent transformational action.
findings.matters: Persistent overspends in a statutory service, combined with unsustainable reliance on agency staff, directly threaten the council's ability to deliver services and maintain financial sustainability without major intervention.
findings.figures: £0.696m overspend 2024/25; £0.375m overspend Q1 2025/26; risk assessment identified £1.38m potential Adult Social Care risks over MTFP period
findings.quote: The Council continues to face significant financial challenges. In 2024/25, the Council reported a net revenue overspend of £985,673 driven largely by pressures in Adult Social Care and Children's Services. A key area of concern remains in the unsustainable and escalating costs within Adult Social Care with the service reporting at the end of Q1 of 2025/26 a further overspend of £375,493 due to increased reliance on agency staff and increased travel and accommodation costs, alongside reduced income.

findings.headline: £20m+ Town Hall Redevelopment project with grant funding issues and pending objection investigation
findings.detail: The Council is engaged in a significant capital programme (Town Hall Redevelopment / Cultural Centre and Museum Project) with estimated final costs over £20m, funded through a blend of public grants and local contributions. The auditor identified that the council did not correctly account for a National Lottery Heritage Fund reimbursement claim of £552,000 in 2024/25 (should have been accrued as income and a debtor). Additionally, an objection from a Local Government Elector has been received requesting a public interest report regarding various aspects of the scheme; the auditor's work on this is nearing completion pending sign-off from PSAA.
findings.matters: A large capital project funded by grants carries execution risk, particularly when grant accounting has been initially incorrect and there are public objections raising questions about the scheme's governance or value for money.
findings.figures: £20m+ estimated final project cost; £552,000 2024/25 National Lottery Heritage Fund reimbursement initially unrecorded
findings.quote: The Council is engaged in a significant capital programme - Town Hall Redevelopment (also known as the Cultural Centre and Museum Project. The estimate of the final costs is over £20m and the funding of the project is through a blend of public grants and local contributions.

findings.headline: Long-standing property valuation accuracy issue requiring prior period adjustment and additional audit work
findings.detail: The council's property valuations have had accuracy problems for several years, specifically around floor area measurements. In 2024/25, a prior period adjustment was made involving the recalculation of floor areas of a number of assets, reclassification of certain assets from Infrastructure to Other Land and Buildings, inclusion of finance lease land, and impairment of six housing assets. The auditor applied additional resources to this area and is still concluding work on property valuations.
findings.matters: Persistent valuation errors undermine the reliability of the balance sheet, particularly for property assets which represent significant portions of the council's asset base and borrowing capacity.
findings.figures: Council housing £10.8m; other land and buildings £28.7m; adjustment involved multiple asset reclassifications
findings.quote: The accuracy of the measurements used by the Council's valuer has been an issue for a number of years and was subject to an External Audit recommendation as far back as 2020/21.

findings.headline: Significant weakness in financial sustainability driven by Adult Social Care cost pressures
findings.detail: The auditor has identified a significant weakness in the Council's arrangements regarding financial sustainability. Cost pressures in Adult Social Care present a significant risk to the Council's financial sustainability. The auditor states that if urgent action is not taken, reserves balances could be depleted very soon. This finding appears in the separate Auditor's Annual Report which accompanies this report.
findings.matters: This is a material control weakness affecting the council's ability to meet its financial obligations and deliver services sustainably, directly impacting creditworthiness and the council's financial position.
findings.figures: Pension fund net liability £3.4m (down from £3.7m); council housing valued at £10.8m; other land and buildings valued at £28.7m
findings.quote: Whilst the Council has taken and continues to take steps to strengthen its medium-term financial resilience, cost pressures in Adult Social Care present a significant risk to the Council's financial sustainability. If urgent action is not taken; reserves balances could be depleted very soon.

findings.paper_title: CIoS Internal Audit Governance Cttee Report - Jan 2026
findings.headline: Cyber security review identified absence of designated IT officer and incomplete staff training
findings.detail: Cyber security audit found two control gaps: no designated officer with IT skills, and officers and members have not adequately completed cyber security training. However, overall cyber security assurance is Reasonable.
findings.matters: Lack of designated IT responsibility and incomplete security training represent control weaknesses that could affect council resilience and data protection.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: Two issues were raised in this review relating to the absence of a designated officer with IT skills and adequate completion of cyber security training for officers and members.

findings.paper_title: CIoS Internal Audit Governance Cttee Report - Jan 2026
findings.headline: Risk management training requirement remains a repeat finding from prior year
findings.detail: Risk management training was identified as a finding in 2024/25 audit and remains unresolved in 2025/26. The council has made progress linking the Risk Register with Corporate Plan and streamlining it to key risks, but training compliance continues to be a gap.
findings.matters: Unresolved control findings from prior audit indicate governance control gaps are not being fixed; this one repeats across consecutive years.
findings.figures: None
findings.quote: We reported two findings covering the opportunity to improve integration with service level risk management and a repeat of our 2024/25 finding covering the requirement for risk management training.

news_drafts.headline: Performance Development Plan completion collapsed from 40% to 18% in a single year
news_drafts.lead: Poor capability planning signals HR management capacity issues and weak workforce development. Failure to recover completion rates after April 2026 process changes would confirm the council lacks internal HR capacity.

news_drafts.headline: Council decision reports regularly late; 3 of 4 quarters exceed 5% non-compliance target
news_drafts.lead: Chronic failure to meet reporting timelines is a governance stress indicator signalling insufficient administrative capacity or process breakdown, both of which matter to lenders assessing organizational stability.

news_drafts.headline: Staff vacancies at 22% with heavy agency reliance in Adult and Children's Social Care
news_drafts.lead: Agency workers cost significantly more than permanent staff, creating hidden cost pressures in the budget. Heavy reliance on agency staff in statutory social care services also creates service delivery and compliance risk.
